course.title: Camday – Cambridge Lower Secondary Science — Stage 7

unit.title: Acids and Alkalis
unit.blurb: Acids and alkalis around us, working safely, testing with indicators and the pH scale, gas tests, and neutralisation.

O1.t: Describe acids, their properties and safe handling, and test for carbon dioxide and hydrogen.

O2.t: Describe alkalis, their uses and properties.

O3.t: Use indicators and the pH scale to classify solutions as acidic, neutral or alkaline.

O4.t: Describe neutralisation and its uses, using pH to follow the change.

captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 8: Acids and Alkalis.
Why does vinegar taste sour?
Why does soap feel slippery?
How can we tell an acid from an alkali without tasting it?
In this unit, we'll explore the acids and alkalis all around us,
and what happens when they meet.
Have you ever tasted vinegar or lemon juice?
That sharp, sour taste comes from acids.
Lemons contain citric acid, and vinegar contains ethanoic acid.
Fizzy drinks contain carbonic acid, and car batteries contain sulfuric acid.
Nitric acid is used to make fertilisers.
Acids are inside living things too.
Your stomach makes hydrochloric acid to kill bacteria and digest food.
Lactic acid builds up in muscles during exercise, vitamin C is ascorbic acid,
and even DNA is an acid!
Rainwater is naturally slightly acidic, because carbon dioxide dissolves in it.
Burning fossil fuels releases acidic pollutants, which make acid rain.
It harms trees and corrodes statues and buildings.
In the school lab, we use dilute acids,
which have been mixed with water to make them weaker.
They can still be dangerous,
so always check the hazard symbol on the bottle first.
This one means corrosive.
Protect yourself and others: wear safety goggles and gloves.
Never pour acid directly; use a dropper.
And never pour water into acid.
Always add the acid slowly to water, to stop it spitting.
If you spill acid on your skin or clothes,
rinse with plenty of water and tell your teacher.
And never taste a substance to find out whether it is an acid!
Acids share some general properties.
Foods that taste sour are usually acidic.
But never taste a substance to test it!
Acids are corrosive: they can damage materials and burn skin.
Acids also conduct electricity,
which is why sulfuric acid is used in car batteries.
Acids change the colour of indicators.
Litmus is an indicator: in an acid, blue litmus paper turns red,
and red litmus stays red.
Acids react with carbonates to produce carbon dioxide gas.
To test for carbon dioxide, bubble it through limewater.
The limewater turns milky.
Acids react with some metals, like magnesium, to produce hydrogen gas.
To test for hydrogen, hold a lighted splint near it:
you'll hear a squeaky pop!
Acids also react with alkalis to make a salt and water only.
This is called neutralisation,
and we'll come back to it later in the unit.
Marble chips are calcium carbonate.
They are dropped into dilute acid,
and the gas is bubbled through clear limewater.
Predict: what will happen to the limewater?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The chips fizz, and bubbles of gas travel along the tube.
After a minute, the clear limewater turns milky.
Explain what you saw.
Acids react with carbonates to make a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas.
Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky, so this is the test for carbon dioxide.
Pause and explain it in your own words.

captions: Alkalis are the chemical opposites of acids.
You use them every day: toothpaste, soap and some antacid tablets contain alkalis.
Strong alkalis clean tough dirt: ammonia solution is used in floor cleaners,
and sodium hydroxide, also called caustic soda, is in oven cleaners.
Alkalis taste bitter and feel soapy, they conduct electricity,
and strong alkalis are corrosive,
so handle them with the same care as acids.
Alkalis turn red litmus blue,
and they react with acids to make a salt and water.
Alkalis are all around your home.
Look at these four products.
Toothpaste is mildly alkaline.
It neutralises the acid that bacteria make in your mouth,
which helps protect your teeth.
Soap is alkaline. That is why it feels slippery,
and it helps lift grease off your skin.
Oven cleaner contains sodium hydroxide, a strong alkali.
It breaks down burnt-on grease, but it is corrosive, so wear gloves.
Antacid tablets contain weak alkalis or carbonates.
They neutralise extra stomach acid and ease indigestion.

captions: An indicator changes colour depending on whether a solution is acidic,
alkaline or neutral. With litmus: acids turn blue litmus red, alkalis turn red litmus blue,
and neutral solutions don't change either colour.
You can make your own indicator!
Chop red cabbage leaves, soak them in hot water for 15 minutes,
then strain and cool the purple juice.
Add the juice to different household liquids and watch the colours change.
Red cabbage juice turns red in acids, stays purple in neutral solutions,
and turns green or yellow in alkalis.
Turmeric is another natural indicator, turning red-orange in alkalis.
Red cabbage juice is purple.
A few drops are added to lemon juice,
pure water and baking soda solution.
Predict: what colour will each cup turn?
Pause and decide.
Watch. The same amount of cabbage juice goes into each cup.
The lemon juice turns red, the water stays purple,
and the baking soda solution turns green.
Explain what you saw.
Red cabbage juice is an indicator.
Lemon juice is an acid, so it turns red.
Water is neutral, so it stays purple.
Baking soda is an alkali, so it turns green.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Litmus tells us whether something is acidic or alkaline,
but not how acidic or alkaline.
For that, we use the pH scale, which runs from 0 to 14.
A pH of 7 is neutral.
Below 7 is acidic, and the lower the number, the stronger the acid.
Above 7 is alkaline, and 14 is the most alkaline.
Battery acid and stomach acid are near the bottom of the scale.
Lemon juice, vinegar, coffee and milk are acidic too.
Pure water sits right at 7.
On the alkaline side, we find baking soda, antacids, ammonia, soap, bleach and,
at the very top, drain cleaner.
To find the pH in the lab, we use Universal Indicator.
Dip the paper in the solution and compare its colour with the chart.
A digital pH meter can also give a reading.
Here are typical pH values of seven everyday substances,
measured with a pH meter.
Lemon juice and vinegar are below 7, so they are acidic.
Milk is only slightly acidic, and pure water is neutral at 7.
Baking soda, soap and ammonia are above 7, so they are alkaline.
Pause and decide: which substance on the chart is the strongest alkali,
and which is the strongest acid?
Some flowers are natural indicators!
Hydrangeas grow blue flowers in acidic soil,
and pink or red flowers in neutral to alkaline soil.
Scientists are even developing indicators for inside the human body.
The area around a cancer tumour is more acidic than healthy tissue.
In 2013, a team led by Dr Franz Schilling found that zymonic
acid responds to pH and can be detected by MRI scans.
This could help doctors see whether a treatment is working.

stops.note: Paused after: “Power stations burning fossil fuels release sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain. They n”

captions: Here is an acid with Universal Indicator: red, about pH 1.
Let's add an alkali, a little at a time.
As alkali is added, the acidity drops and the pH rises.
When exactly the right amounts of acid and alkali are mixed,
the pH reaches 7 and the solution is neutral.
This is neutralisation: acid plus alkali gives a salt plus water.
For example, hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide make sodium chloride, table salt,
and water.
Add even more alkali, and the solution becomes alkaline.
To hit pH 7 exactly,
chemists use a burette to add the alkali drop by drop.
This method is called titration.
Keep adding alkali after neutralisation, and the pH keeps rising:
the solution turns blue-purple, because now it is alkaline.
An alkali is added to 20 cubic centimetres of dilute acid,
and the pH is measured after each addition.
At first the pH rises only slowly,
because there is still plenty of acid left.
Then, close to 20 cubic centimetres, the pH jumps very quickly through 7,
the neutral point. After that, the solution is alkaline.
Pause and decide: how much alkali was needed to neutralise the acid exactly?
Neutralisation is very useful.
Too much stomach acid causes indigestion, or heartburn.
Antacid tablets contain alkalis or carbonates that neutralise the extra acid.
Power stations burning fossil fuels release sulfur dioxide, which causes acid rain.
They neutralise it with an alkali, calcium hydroxide, in a process called scrubbing.
Lakes and soils made too acidic by acid rain
can be treated with alkaline substances like lime,
so plants and animals can thrive again.
Farmers check the soil's pH for their crops.
Even your hair care uses neutralisation!
Many shampoos are alkaline, and conditioners are slightly acidic,
so together they neutralise each other, leaving hair soft and smooth.
Now it is your turn to shine!
